prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its development into long-acting incretin therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part B023 prize to Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. The chair's first question is who holds the third place. My answer is that the achievement the committee can defend most firmly is the whole chain from the physiology of proglucagon-derived peptides and the incretin effect (Holst, Drucker) to the pharmacological solution of a peptide with a half-life of minutes (Knudsen's acylated, albumin-binding analogues). The citation therefore names both the physiology and the development of long-acting therapies. The decade of independent outcome trials in glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal disease shows why the chain matters, and no member disputes maturity. On the second question, I think a company-based development scientist alongside two academic discoverers is acceptable here: the design of the long-acting molecule is a conceptual and experimental step in its own right, and it is what turned the biology into medicine. I do not see a reason to add a second part. Nothing in round 1 shows a second achievement that is both clean in credit and clearly strong enough to share the prize this year.
statement.case_against: Credit remains the weak point. Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is a real claim that I leave out, Habener and Bell are outside the supplied names, and a three-person cap cannot be fully fair to everyone in this history. The prize can also be read as a compound of academic physiology and industrial development, which is a fair objection. If the committee decided the prize should reward discovery only, my configuration would be the weaker one and Mojsov would replace Knudsen. The alternatives have their own faults. Optogenetics (B001) is mature but has six claimants for three places and a medical impact that is mostly as a research tool. The unfolded protein response (B051) has the cleanest attribution, but the least direct clinical consequence.

responses.point: Perlmann keeps Mojsov in the trio, would hold the citation to the physiology and the active peptide rather than the drug, and says a prize with cleaner attribution may be the fallback if the peptide credit cannot be settled.
responses.response: I take the point that a prize resting on the physiology alone would be the narrower and more traditional one, and that Mojsov's identification of the active peptide is a genuine contribution. I still prefer Knudsen for the third place, for two reasons. The chair's question on documentation matters: nothing in the supplied record settles priority among Mojsov, Habener and Bell, and I do not want a prize to depend on a point we have all said we cannot resolve. And your own case against concedes that without long-acting analogues the biology would not have become a treatment. If the citation were limited to the peptide, the evidence of importance would sit outside the prize. I do not accept that cleaner attribution justifies abandoning B023. The attribution risk is a reason to word the citation carefully, not to move away from the strongest scientific case.

responses.point: El Manira holds that the configuration should carry both halves, the physiology and the drug, and says he cannot resolve Mojsov's role or the objection that crediting Knudsen rewards optimisation rather than discovery.
responses.response: We agree on the structure. I want to answer the optimisation objection directly, since you and I both raise it. Acylation and albumin binding to extend half-life is a design principle that was tested and carried through to a drug, so I regard it as discovery-level work in the medical sense, not routine tuning. I also agree that no one can settle Mojsov's role from the supplied record, and that is the reason I would not make her inclusion the hinge. Where I differ slightly is on the second alternative. You hold B022 as a backup and I hold B051, because I weigh attribution clarity alongside clinical reach. I would not object to B022 as a fallback, but Eshhar's omission is a credit problem I find as serious as the GLP-1 one.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius notes that pairing basic physiology with industrial development makes a compound recognition, that any three-person split leaves out someone, and that long-term safety of the class beyond weight and glucose is still being defined.
responses.response: I agree that the compound character is the real cost of this configuration, and that is why I considered splitting it into two achievements. On balance I reject the split. Physiology and drug are one continuous chain, and dividing them would cost laureate places without improving fairness. On long-term safety, I take the point but do not think it counts against awarding the prize now. The prize recognises a discovery that has already shown large, independently confirmed benefit, and open questions about long-term effects beyond weight and glucose are normal for a mature drug class. They would matter if the claim were for a specific agent, which the citation avoids. I would accept wording that says 'therapies' and not individual drugs.

responses.point: The chair frames the trio as dependent on whether the committee wants to reward the physiology, the drug design or the combination, and holds B051 and B001 as possible second parts.
responses.response: I answer your questions in order. The committee should reward the combination, with the citation wording above. A one-part prize is defensible as a compound if the citation makes the chain explicit, since a split would produce two parts that each fall short on credit or scope. For a second part, I would not pair B023 with B001 this year, because no three-name subset of Boyden, Bamberg, Nagel, Miesenboeck, Deisseroth and Hegemann leaves out fewer than three people with strong claims. For B051, the Mori and Walter pairing is clean, but the division of early unfolded protein response credit rests on my recollection and not on the supplied record, and the clinical consequence is the thinnest among the shortlist. So I would hold B051 and B001 as alternatives and not add either to the preferred prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can credit the identification of the active GLP-1 peptide fairly without Mojsov and without Habener or Bell, who are outside the supplied names.
Whether a company-based development scientist is accepted by the full committee as a co-laureate, and whether the citation wording is enough to answer the compound-recognition objection.
Whether my recollection of how early unfolded protein response credit divides between Mori and Walter, and others, would hold up against the full record.
Whether optogenetics can ever be given a defensible three-person credit that does not leave out Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenboeck.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My documented connections (spatial transcriptomics, single-cell and brain-atlas co-authors, and eight recorded co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg, not independently audited) do not involve any shortlisted candidate's credited names, and the round-1 exchange raised no new tie. I see no need for recusal on any shortlisted candidate.
